summary: Tsavorite is the vivid green grossular garnet from East Africa, a rare, brilliant gem of growth, prosperity and a renewed heart in crystal lore.
intro: Tsavorite is the intense green variety of grossular garnet, colored by traces of vanadium and chromium. Its brilliance and vivid, leafy green rival those of emerald, but tsavorite is usually much cleaner and more durable, with a hardness of about 7 to 7.5. Crystals are generally small, so faceted stones above two carats are rare and prized. The gem is found only in a few places, mainly in Tanzania and Kenya, near the Tsavo National Park that gave the stone its name. Because of its limited supply, tsavorite is expensive, though it is becoming increasingly popular with jewelry designers who love its vivid, fresh color.
history: Tsavorite was discovered in the late 1960s by the Scottish geologist Campbell Bridges in the Lelatema Mountains of Tanzania. Because of export restrictions, he later found a deposit in Kenya near Tsavo National Park, and Tiffany and Company, led by Henry Platt, introduced the name tsavorite and promoted the gem in the early 1970s. The name tsavorite was adopted for the stone, replacing earlier names like green grossular. Bridges's pioneering work in dangerous mining conditions became legendary in the gem trade. Though the gem is still young compared to others, it has become one of the most coveted green stones in modern jewelry.
meaning: Tsavorite is the garnet of green renewal. Crystal practitioners link it to the Heart chakra and use it to cultivate growth, new beginnings, and a hopeful, open attitude. Its lively green is said to refresh the spirit and support a sense of abundance, particularly through steady, ethical effort. Many people choose it as a gem of prosperity and as a symbol of nature's renewal in spring. It is also associated with warmth in relationships, a bright and sincere kind of love. As a rare and durable stone, tsavorite is often chosen for meaningful jewelry as a talisman of a fresh start. The energy is described as vibrant but calm, like sunlight on new leaves.
howToUse: Wear tsavorite as a ring, pendant, or earrings to keep its fresh green energy close. Hold a stone during heart meditation, imagining green light spreading from the center of your chest. Place a piece on your desk to support steady growth in your projects. Combine with green aventurine and citrine in a prosperity grid. Gift a tsavorite to mark a new job, a new home, or a new chapter. Keep a small stone in the garden shed or near houseplants as a symbol of flourishing.
care: Tsavorite is durable at Mohs 7 to 7.5. Wash it with lukewarm soapy water and a soft brush. Ultrasonic cleaners are generally safe for clean stones. Cleanse by running water, sunlight, moonlight, sound, or smoke. It is stable in sunlight. Store apart from diamonds and sapphires to prevent scratches. Because stones are usually clean, they hold up well in rings, though a hard knock can still chip an edge.
identify: Tsavorite is a vivid green, singly refractive stone with strong brilliance and few inclusions. Emerald is usually more included and softer in tone, green tourmaline shows doubling, and peridot is more yellowish with a lower hardness. Demantoid is a different green garnet with horsetail inclusions and more fire. Green glass and synthetic stones are common imitators. Tsavorite is usually untreated, and heating is not typical. Origin is often noted on lab reports.

faq.a: Tsavorite is the vivid green variety of grossular garnet, colored by vanadium and chromium. It was discovered in East Africa in the 1960s and named after Kenya's Tsavo National Park.
Neither is better, but tsavorite is typically cleaner and a bit harder, with more brilliance and fewer fractures. Emerald has a softer, velvety look and a much longer history in jewelry and lore.
Tsavorite is traditionally linked to renewal, prosperity, and a hopeful heart. People use it to support growth and a fresh start, and link its green color with the Heart chakra.
